Hell's Kitchen transcends the limitations of the jukebox format to become something more cohesive and emotionally resonant.
Hell's Kitchen vividly extrapolates an artist's vision into a satisfying Broadway hit.

In the end, audiences should still go crazy for Hell's Kitchen.
The national tour of Alicia Keys ' HELL'S KITCHEN has arrived at the Eccles Theater in Salt Lake City with swagger and soul.
And yet: Hell’s Kitchen is irresistible.
It is an exuberant, moving celebration of art, ambition, family, and the people who help you find your voice.

Hell's Kitchen never quite finds the emotional complexity its best ideas promise. But when this cast launches into another impeccably sung Alicia Keys banger, those shortcomings become surprisingly easy to forgive.
HELL'S KITCHEN catches that current almost immediately.
Another village did envision this show and did a damn good job. Too bad a sound system let them all down.
At its core, “Hell’s Kitchen” understands and even celebrates the passion and pain of both sides of the parent-teen dynamic, and it is that which elevates the show to a “must-see” in my book.
Most striking about this show is the way it finds an emotional core in Keys' songs, from the biggest hits to deeper cuts, that feels authentic to the story rather than forced or gratuitous.
“Hell’s Kitchen” is an intimate, moving, and exciting show, filled with powerful performances and enough well-known hits that it’ll be difficult for many to remain seated.
Put it all together with the power of the performances and the audience is willingly and unwittingly transported.
Alicia Keys' fans shouldn't miss 'Hell's Kitchen.' Musical theater fans who love a story that goes down easy and songs they know performed in new, exciting ways, shouldn't miss it, either.
Actually, that “fire” is true of this entire production of Hell’s Kitchen at the Broward Center—including the top-flight acting, singing, precision dancing and production values.
Fortunately Hell's Kitchen was able to break down all those barriers and provide a captivating night of theater.
Every ensemble number is a joy.
This was a wonderful night out at the Theater.
This isn't only a story about a book that occasionally can't keep up with its songs.
The music is not just decoration. It is character, conflict, and catharsis.
It is undoubtedly one of the strongest examples of what a “jukebox musical” is and what they can deliver as a piece of musical theatre.
The hits are still hitting … and hitting hard.

That’s just one highlight of the show, which opened Thursday, May 7, at ATG San Francisco’s Orpheum Theatre with one of the best ensembles of singing voices in any touring cast to visit the Bay Area in recent memory.
Where the film zipped along, the musical feels more earthbound, and some of the humour — particularly in the café and Amélie’s neighbourhood — feels laboured.
Alas the sound unbalance made most of the lyrics incomprehensible.

Keys' songs are frequently used effectively, and the production has striking scenic design and energetic choreography, but a clunky first act, sound balance issues and a story built around familiar coming-of-age beats keep the musical from fully catching fire.

cn.t: Critics praise Hell's Kitchen as an electrifying musical that transcends typical jukebox fare, with Alicia Keys' songbook organically woven into a compelling coming-of-age story and elevated by knockout vocal performances from the touring cast.
